lessons.title: The E Format
intro: Science deals with huge and tiny numbers: the speed of light is 299,800,000 m/s, an electron weighs 0.000…0009 grams. F format can't hold those.
E format prints them in scientific notation: 0.2998E+09 means 0.2998 × 10⁹. E12.4 uses 12 columns and shows 4 digits.
On the card, E-numbers work too: 2.998E8 is a perfectly good FORTRAN number.

exercises.prompt: Which format fits the mass of the Earth, 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg?
exercises.explanation: E format handles any size in a few columns.

exercises.prompt: How is 2.998E8 written as a normal number?
exercises.explanation: Move the decimal point 8 places to the right.

exercises.prompt: Print X in scientific notation with 4 digits.
exercises.explanation: E for exponent, then width and digits.

exercises.prompt: What does F8.2 print for a value too big to fit, like 123456789.0?
exercises.explanation: When a number doesn't fit its field, FORTRAN fills it with stars. Time to switch to E format.

exercises.prompt: Why does E format need more columns than digits?
options: Room for the sign, 0., and the exponent like E+09
exercises.explanation: E12.4 shows 4 digits, but the whole field is 12 columns wide.

lessons.title: Repeat Counts and Groups
intro: A number in front of a format item repeats it: 3I5 is the same as I5, I5, I5. Brackets repeat whole groups: 2(I3, F6.1) means I3, F6.1, I3, F6.1.
If the WRITE list has more values than the format, FORTRAN starts a new line and uses the format again. One FORMAT (1X, 5I4) can print 20 numbers as four rows.
Short formats meant fewer columns on the card, and every card counted.

exercises.explanation: The number in front repeats the item.

exercises.prompt: How many lines does the example print?
exercises.explanation: 10 values, 5 per line: the format is used twice.
Three per line, and FORTRAN starts a new line for the rest.
The whole group is repeated, in order.

exercises.prompt: This job stops with *ERROR*. Which card is wrong?
exercises.explanation: X is REAL, but the format only has I fields. Use F, like 3F6.1.

exercises.prompt: What is the advantage of FORMAT (1X, 5I4) over five separate WRITEs?
options: One card prints the whole array, in neat columns
It's the only way to print integers
exercises.explanation: Fewer cards, and the columns line up by themselves.

lessons.title: Printing a Report
intro: A good printout has a title, column headers and lined-up numbers. Headers are FORMATs with text; the data lines use matching widths, so everything sits under its header.
The first character of every line still controls the printer: blank means next line, 0 means skip a line first, 1 starts a new page. Reports started with 1 so each one began on a fresh page.
Computer centers printed thousands of pages a day on wide, fan-folded paper with green stripes, so your eyes could follow a line across.

exercises.prompt: What does a 0 as the first character of a line do?
exercises.explanation: 0 = double spacing. 1 = new page. Blank = next line.

exercises.prompt: Why do the header and the data line use the same widths?
options: So the numbers line up under their headers
exercises.explanation: '   N  N**2' has N at column 4 and N**2 ending at column 10, matching I4 and I6.

exercises.prompt: Start the report on a new page.
exercises.explanation: A 1 in the first position: the printer jumps to the top of the next page.

exercises.prompt: What does the / in FORMAT (' SQUARES'/' ', '   N  N**2') do?
options: Ends the first line, so the headers go on a second line
exercises.explanation: Each / starts a new line in the same WRITE.

exercises.prompt: Stack the cards for a report with a header and the numbers 1 to 3.
exercises.explanation: The header first, outside the loop, then one line per number.

exercises.prompt: Why was printer paper striped green and white?
options: To help the eye follow long lines across the page
exercises.explanation: "Greenbar paper" was the look of computing for 30 years.
